newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Former EU farm chiefs deny BSE cover-up.
newsitem.headline: Former EU farm chiefs deny BSE cover-up.

text.p: Two former European Union farm commissioners on Tuesday strongly rejected allegations that they tried to cover up the human health risk from mad cow disease.
Giving evidence to a European Parliament committee of inquiry, Irishman Ray MacSharry and Luxembourger Rene Steichen said they had always given priority to protecting public health.

"Rumour and gossip and innuendo and allegation printed, repeated and constantly said becomes established as facts in some people's minds," Irishman Ray MacSharry, farm commissioner between 1989-93, angrily told the inquiry.

"I would like to know if this committee is conducting this inquiry or whether Liberation is doing it on their behalf," added MacSharry who masterminded a sweeping reform of the EU's costly farm policy in 1992.

On Tuesday, the French daily said a joint investigation with the Irish Times found new evidence that MacSharry and the Commission's French director general for agriculture, Guy Legras, had played key roles in an alleged cover-up.
Liberation published what it said was a copy of a note written by Legras after a meeting with MacSharry saying "BSE: stop any meeting."
Legras denied any campaign to conceal information when he appeared before the parliamentary committee on October 1, saying he did not take MacSharry's remark seriously.
MacSharry, who was in charge of EU farm affairs when mad cow disease, or Bovine Spongiform Encephalopathy (BSE), peaked in 1992, said he had never given orders to hush up the problem.
The fatal cattle brain disease has struck down 165,000 cattle in Britain, where it was first reported in 1986. Fewer than 600 cases have been reported in other European countries.
The EU banned British beef exports in March, 1996, after the British government said the epidemic could spread to people who ate infected beef.
"I had never at any time exercised any pressure on anybody not to in any way disclose fully any information regarding this particular problem," MacSharry said.
Luxembourger Steichen, who succeeded MacSharry as farm commissioner between 1993-95, was also categoric.
"Neither myself, nor my staff, concealed anything or tried to hush up discussions," he said.

Both Steichen and MacSharry stressed that in the early 1990s scientists had advised that there was only a remote threat to human health from BSE and the action the EU had taken was both correct and timely.
Both MacSharry and Steichen said they had fought to increase the number of EU veterinary inspectors but were resisted by member states.
It was up to member states to ensure that a ban on meat and bone meal in animal feed and other EU rules to eradicate BSE were respected, they insisted.
Steichen said he resisted British pressure to ease conditions for deboning meat in order to reduce the BSE risk.
He added Britain had difficulty identifying and tracking animal movements.
"The English don't have personal identity cards, perhaps that's why they don't want to give one to cows," he noted.
